newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian insurance giant plans listing in 1998.
newsitem.headline: Australian insurance giant plans listing in 1998.

text.p: Australia's giant insurance and funds management group, the Australian Mutual Provident Society (AMP), on Thursday announced a plan to list on the Australian, New Zealand and possibly U.K. stock exchanges by late 1998.

AMP, the world's 15th largest life insurance company with about A$90 billion of assets, dominates the local investment scene and holds more than three percent of the Australian share market on behalf of its five million customers.
It would rank among the top 10 listed companies with a huge shareholder register of more than two million and a market capitalisation estimated by analysts to be about A$10 billion.

"Management and the board firmly believe that the demutualisation is in the best interests of the members and the policyholders of AMP," managing director and chief executive George Trumbull told reporters at a news conference.
Trumbull, hired from an executive position with U.S. insurance group CIGNA in 1994, said AMP policyholders who now own the mutual firm would vote on the proposal in the second half of 1997.
He also revealed that AMP was ready to go on the acquisition trail, with the ability to spend up to A$5 billion on non-bank takeovers in the United Kingdom or United States.
AMP already operates the large Pearl Assurance group in the U.K., which it purchased in 1989 and now has about A$38 billion of assets.

The plan by AMP follows a similar move by its second-placed insurance rival National Mutual Holdings Ltd, which listed on the share market in October and is valued at A$3.04 billion. National Mutual is 51 percent-controlled by French insurer Axa.
Trumbull said the favoured listing path would involve the formation of a holding company which would own the existing AMP structure.
"We would certainly expect to rank in the top 10 in Australian market value, but stock market conditions at the time we list are going to dictate what the actual market capitalisation is," he said.

In today's terms, AMP members' capital would be worth A$8 billion to A$10 billion (US$6.34 billion to US$7.93 billion) in 1998. But how this would translate into market value was not predictable, Trumbull said.
AMP had not decided whether or not to raise capital when it listed, but a raising may depend on whether it needed to finance any further acquisitions, he said.
AMP could handle a non-bank purchase in the A$2 billion to A$5 billion range "without any trouble", Trumbull said.
"It may be between now and then we've actually been successful on a couple of the big acquisitions we're working on."
Trumbull said he would prefer big rather than small takeovers.
"Small is a bigger pain in the ass than big, so why not do big. Doing small ones is more work than doing big ones."

"We think pension, savings, asset management, risk management, where we have substantive skills, are markets with varying degrees of attractiveness in the developed English-speaking countries -- the U.K., the U.S. and New Zealand," he said.
AMP would likely protect itself from hostile takeover for the first five years after listing by limiting individual and institutional shareholdings to a maximum of five percent, Trumbull said.
